, had been posted to Instagram by Council Member (CM) Sandra Sepulveda, the chief sponsor of an ordinance to restrict the use of drone surveillance technology.

Reached for comment, CM Sepulveda said that she believes the drone "demonstration" was directly in response to her legislation, which had also prompted Chief Drake to write a letter urging Council Members to not further limit his department's access to drone surveillance tools, a form of AI-powered corporate mass surveillance that MNPD has already shown they are willing to implement on a "trial" basis without proper authorization.

When members of the media, Metro staffers, and community members arrived at MNPD HQ to attend the presentation on Friday, they were turned away by security and told that it was an "invite-only" meeting.
Also turned away were several members of the Metro Community Review Board, who by WSMV's account had been caught off guard to learn the trial launched without Council approval.

tokens.c: It is not clear why a newly minted reporter was the only civilian besides the lobbyist Sam Reed who was allowed to attend the meeting, which is concerning given the stakes of AI-powered corporate mass surveillance.

Council Members also reported talking to a lawyer from the Council's legal office after learning the public would not be allowed in, as they were concerned about the TOMA implications and if attending such a meeting could result in ethics complaints or litigation. According to a Council Member present, after ten minutes of research conducted right before the meeting took place, the representative of the Council's legal office reportedly concluded that Tennessee's Open Meetings Act (TOMA) did not apply since this was a "training" and therefore it did not need to be open to the public.
Upon entering the building, CM Nash, a former MNPD commander, denied to me this private meeting violated TOMA, claiming that they were not going to be talking about any legislation.
"Is this meeting about police drones?" I asked him.
"Yes." He replied.
"Is there open legislation regarding the restriction of police drones currently on the Council floor?"
"Yes," he said.
But this meeting about police drones, had nothing to do with any legislation about those very same police drones, he insisted.
It was not clear why, if there was no lobbying about legislation going on, there was a lobbyist invited to this closed door meeting.
The police officer manning the door confirmed to me that the lobbyist Sam Reed was "on the list."

When I contacted Mr. Reed by phone about what was going on and indicated I knew he was present and asked for his assistance attending the demonstration, he promptly exited the building and left the premises before the demonstration began.

Sam Reed is a registered Metro Nashville lobbyist for Elon Musk Boring Company, Vanderbilt University, The Nashville Downtown Partnership, Oracle, and Nate Bargatze's eponymous theme park "Nateland" the comedian is attempting to build.

tokens.c: Friday's analysis that advised Council Members it was proper to attend a closed door demonstration about the benefits of drones with other Council Members while drone legislation is actively on the Council floor, is particularly concerning to some. Other recent examples have demonstrated concerning patterns from the Counsel's legal office.

It was Council's legal office, someone familiar with the situation told this outlet, that gave the legal opinion that the Nashville Downtown Partnership only needed to change their budget by one dollar to resubmit its rejected budget to Council
— a decision that has also raised eyebrows about the Council's legal office.
The Council legal office has had new leadership since
longtime Counsel Margaret Darby departed the role in December 2025 at the end of her four-year contract, moving to private practice

q.s-banner-darby-departure: the end of her four-year contract

tokens.c: and there is concern it is not giving legal advice with the public's best interest and the spirit of the law in mind.
Researchers like Ed Vogel from the Lucy Parsons Lab,
featured in the Nashville Banner's Aug. 6 piece on the airport's under-the-radar license plate readers, has said these fights ultimately come down to democracy

are documenting how procurement laws and sunshine acts are being shredded to adopt the move-fast-and-break-things approach through which AI-powered corporate mass surveillance is brought in through every side door available.
At stake, Vogel puts it, is democracy.

Friday's secret meeting, led by MNPD's Deputy Chief Gilder, is only the latest in a long string of bypassing all norms and accountability to provide a panopticon to police, and more to the point, the corporate surveillance firms acquiring the footage and cashing the checks.

As the meeting detailed to Council members, MNPD has been flying drones for the better part of two months without a single contract in place saying what a war drone manufacturer may do with the footage it has obtained of thousands of Nashvillians.

Friday's chaotic secret meeting is now becoming a standard sight around the country, with AI-powered corporate mass surveillance being pushed by product marketers and, increasingly, the thin blue line between sales people and public safety officers is being blurred.
